title: QuanFraud: Quantum State Veriﬁcation Scheme for Fraud Detection in IoT-Assisted Quantum-Blockchain Networks
abstract_summary: The paper presents QuanFraud, a protocol that combines GHZ–θ quantum state verification, Decentralized Identifiers (DID), and a Quantum Support Vector Classifier (QSVC) within an auditable blockchain framework to provide verifiable, tamper-evident fraud detection for IoT-assisted financial systems. Evaluated on a 20k-record financial dataset using PCA, SMOTE, and nested 10-fold validation, classical models achieve higher balanced accuracy (~77%) while QSVC attains ~42%, but QuanFraud prioritizes NISQ-ready verifiability, kernel-level privacy, identity binding, and on-chain auditability over raw accuracy.
methodology_description: The authors propose and experimentally evaluate QuanFraud, a hybrid quantum–classical, assurance-first fraud-detection pipeline for IoT-assisted quantum-blockchain networks. The methodology couples identity governance (Decentralized Identifiers and Hyperledger AnonCreds) and immutable on-chain logging with quantum channel integrity checks (GHZ state preparation and θ-protocol verification) before ingestion by a machine-learning classifier. Data preprocessing uses normalization, PCA dimensionality reduction, K-means clustering, and SMOTE oversampling to correct class imbalance. Only samples whose associated n-qubit GHZ entangled resource pass a fidelity check (FGHZ >= 0.5 via the θ-protocol) are forwarded to the quantum encoding stage. Quantum feature encoding uses a ZZ-Feature-Map (pairwise Z⊗Z entanglers) into a shallow variational circuit (trainable ansatz composed of Ry, Rz rotations and CX entanglers); measurements produce scores which are calibrated (Platt/Isotonic) and thresholded (decision threshold K* chosen by inner CV maximizing F1/BA). The evaluation employs a leakage-safe nested cross-validation protocol (outer 10-fold for unbiased test, inner 5-fold for hyperparameter/threshold tuning), reports a full metric set (balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC, PR-AUC, Recall, F1, ECE), and compares QSVC/VQC performance against classical baselines (Random Forest, XGBoost). Experiments are run on classical hardware with Qiskit simulators (IBM Quantum simulator) and a blockchain/AnonCreds testbed (Hyperledger/Indy, Ethereum/Geth in VirtualBox). The methodology emphasizes verifiability (GHZ–θ), identity binding (DID), kernel-level privacy (QSVC), and auditable decision receipts over raw accuracy.
experimental_setup: Classical host: AMD Ryzen 5 5600U running Ubuntu 18.04.4, Python 3.6, Pandas, Jupyter. Quantum experiments executed on IBM Qiskit simulator / IBM Quantum (simulator back-end). Blockchain and identity components run in VirtualBox (Hyperledger Indy/AnonCreds and Ethereum Geth on Ropsten). Vitis HLS 2021.2 used for synchronization. Experiments performed with nested cross-validation and end-to-end timing reported (~45 s runtime for full pipeline in the reported configuration).
dataset_used: A publicly available financial bank-fraud dataset (Kaggle: 'fraud-detection bank dataset - 20k records') containing 20,468 records and 117 features; classes imbalanced (~27% positive class, ~73% negative). The dataset was merged with dynamically generated DID and wallet metadata (DID_Wallet_metadata.csv) to produce sample.csv used for training/testing.

pipeline_steps: 1) Identity and schema registration: Devices obtain DIDs; issuer registers credential definitions in Verifiable Data Registry; smart contract records device DIDs on-chain.
2) Devices transmit CSV telemetry to the quantum network.
3) Preprocessing: normalization, PCA, K-means clustering, SMOTE to rebalance classes.

4) GHZ state preparation (n-qubit, default 4-qubit instantiation described) and fidelity check via the θ-protocol: verifier samples angles {θ_i} summing to multiple of π, parties measure in rotated basis, acceptance if parity condition holds; accept if F_GHZ >= 0.5.
5) For validated samples, encode features into quantum states using ZZ-Feature-Map.
6) Apply trainable variational ansatz (parameterized Ry and Rz rotations and CX entanglers).
7) Measure in Z-basis to obtain measurement outcomes; compute fraud score S_i = f(m_i, θ).
8) Calibrate scores (Platt or Isotonic) using in-fold calibration.
9) Choose decision threshold K* from inner CV (maximizing F1 / Balanced Accuracy).
10) Log validated results and metadata on-chain (Device_DID, timestamp, F_GHZ, predicted label, hash of input).

Cross-validation and tuning: Nested CV with outer 10-fold for test, inner 5-fold for hyperparameter and threshold tuning; metrics aggregated with 95% CIs (DeLong for ROC-AUC, BCa bootstrap for other metrics).

results_summary: QuanFraud is presented as an "assurance-first" fraud-detection protocol combining GHZ–θ quantum-state verification, DID/AnonCreds identity binding, a QSVC-based quantum-classical learner, and blockchain logging. Empirical evaluation on a 20,468-record financial dataset (117 features) with PCA, SMOTE, and rigorous nested CV shows that the QSVC module attains only modest balanced accuracy (~41.6% / 42.1 ± 2.8%), while classical baselines (Random Forest, XGBoost) achieve substantially higher balanced accuracy (>77%). The work demonstrates GHZ–θ checks (fidelity threshold 0.5) and an implemented prototype (Hyperledger AnonCreds + Qiskit simulations), and argues the value of verifiability, auditability, and kernel-space privacy despite the absence of classification accuracy improvements from the quantum component. Time/complexity measures and a composite Trust Score (Strust = 5) are reported to support claims of deployment-readiness under NISQ constraints, while formal security proofs and large-scale hardware validation are left for future work.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not demonstrate a quantum computational or predictive advantage. Empirically, the quantum classifier (QSVC) under NISQ constraints performed substantially worse than classical baselines on balanced accuracy. The authors frame the contribution as verifiability, auditability, and identity assurance (GHZ–θ, DID, blockchain) rather than improved accuracy or demonstrated quantum speedup; therefore a claim of quantum advantage is not applicable.

key_ideas: #idea:near-term-feasibility — QuanFraud explicitly targets NISQ-era deployment: uses shallow variational ansatz, ZZ-feature-map encoding, and fidelity-based GHZ (θ-protocol) checks to gate samples before classification.

#idea:hybrid-approach — End-to-end hybrid pipeline couples classical preprocessing (normalization, PCA, K-means, SMOTE) with quantum feature encoding and a QSVC/VQC classifier; classical optimizer and calibration (Platt/Isotonic) used for parameter tuning and decision-threshold selection.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum experiments were executed on Qiskit/IBM simulators (no results on physical QPUs), and blockchain/identity components were tested in VM testbeds.

#limitation:qubit-count — PCA dimension reduction was used to map features to available qubits (default 4-qubit GHZ instantiation described); approach depends on severe dimensionality reduction to fit current/quasi-NISQ resource constraints.

#limitation:noise — The protocol includes GHZ fidelity checks (accept if F_GHZ >= 0.5) to filter noisy/contaminated sessions, indicating sensitivity to quantum channel noise and limited noise mitigation beyond gating.

#limitation:data-encoding — Feature encoding relies on a ZZ-Feature-Map and mentions explored amplitude/angle encodings and re-uploading; the paper highlights encoding choices as a practical trade-off but does not overcome encoding cost for high-dimensional financial data.

#contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — Empirical results show classical baselines (Random Forest, XGBoost) substantially outperform QSVC (classical BA >77% vs QSVC BA ≈42%), undercutting claims that current quantum classifiers provide accuracy advantages on this financial fraud dataset.

#contradiction:scalability — Although framed as 'NISQ-ready' and verifiability-focused, the methodology relies on simulator experiments, small-qubit GHZ checks, and heavy classical preprocessing, casting doubt on near-term scalability to production-scale financial datasets without loss of utility.
contradictions: The paper's results show classical models (Random Forest, XGBoost) achieve >77% balanced accuracy while the QSVC attains ≈42% BA, contradicting any claim that the applied quantum classifier outperforms classical baselines on this fraud dataset.

QuanFraud emphasizes NISQ readiness and verifiability via GHZ-θ checks but provides only simulator-based quantum experiments and relies on aggressive PCA/SMOTE preprocessing and small-qubit instantiations, which contradicts assertions that the approach scales to real-world, high-dimensional financial workloads without substantial classical support or hardware improvements.
